traditions.name: Shaolin / Chan Buddhist Monastic Practice
traditions.blurb: Combines physical discipline, breath control, and meditation developed by Shaolin monks for both combat readiness and inner stillness.

traditions.name: Ancient Chinese / Taoist & TCM
traditions.blurb: Traditional Chinese Medicine and Taoist practices focused on qi (vital energy) balance, seasonal living, and food-as-medicine.

traditions.name: Mexican / Indigenous (Nahua & Maya-descended)
traditions.blurb: Practices rooted in Nahua and Maya-descended traditions, including curanderismo (traditional healing), temazcal (sweat lodge), and plant medicine.

traditions.name: Buddhism (Theravada & Zen)
traditions.blurb: Meditation and mindfulness techniques focused on awareness, emotional regulation, and mental clarity.

traditions.name: Ayurveda
traditions.blurb: India's traditional system of medicine focused on daily routines (dinacharya), constitution types (doshas), and diet as the foundation of wellness.

traditions.name: Japanese Zen & Nature Practice
traditions.blurb: Zen meditation practices and nature-based rituals developed for mental clarity and stress reduction.

traditions.name: Stoicism
traditions.blurb: A philosophical practice (Epictetus, Seneca, Marcus Aurelius) focused on mental discipline, perspective-taking, and separating what is and isn't in your control.

traditions.name: Nordic & Sámi Traditions
traditions.blurb: Practices rooted in Nordic and Sámi (Indigenous Arctic) life, centered on cold exposure, communal warmth, and rhythm with harsh seasonal light/dark cycles.

traditions.name: West African / Yoruba-Descended Traditions
traditions.blurb: Practices from Yoruba and broader West African traditions, including rhythm/drumming for emotional release, communal ritual, and ancestral connection practices.

techniques.title: Zhan Zhuang (Standing Meditation)
techniques.description: A stillness practice where you hold a relaxed standing posture, building internal strength, grounding, and focus without visible movement.
steps: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, knees slightly bent.
Round your arms as if hugging a large tree, hands at chest height.
Relax shoulders down, tuck chin slightly, keep spine long.
Hold the posture, breathing naturally through the nose, for 3-10 minutes.
Focus attention on sensations in the arms and lower belly (dantian).

techniques.title: Eight Pieces of Brocade (Baduanjin)
techniques.description: A sequence of eight gentle movements paired with breath, traditionally used as a short daily set to circulate energy and loosen the body.
steps: Movement 1: 'Two Hands Hold Up the Heavens' — reach arms overhead on inhale, lower on exhale.
Movement 2: 'Draw the Bow' — mimic drawing a bow side to side, opens chest.
Continue through the remaining six movements at a slow, breath-paced tempo (full sequences widely documented).
Repeat the full set 1-3 times, always syncing breath to movement.

techniques.title: Diaphragmatic Combat Breathing
techniques.description: Deep belly breathing used by monks to stay calm and generate power during physical exertion, adaptable as a stress-response reset.
steps: Place one hand on the belly, one on the chest.
Inhale through the nose, expanding the belly (not the chest) for a count of 4.
Hold briefly for a count of 2.
Exhale slowly through the mouth for a count of 6.
Repeat for 10 cycles.

techniques.title: Hegu (LI4) Acupressure Point
techniques.description: A self-massage point on the hand traditionally used to relieve headaches, stress, and tension.
steps: Locate the point in the webbing between thumb and index finger.
Using the opposite thumb, press firmly into the point.
Massage in small circles for 30-60 seconds.
Switch hands and repeat.
Note: traditionally avoided during pregnancy.

techniques.title: Five-Element Food Energetics
techniques.description: TCM classifies foods as warming, cooling, or neutral, and matches them to season and individual constitution rather than fixed nutrition rules.
steps: In cold months or if often feeling cold/fatigued, favor warming foods: ginger, cinnamon, cooked stews, bone broth.
In hot months or if often feeling irritable/inflamed, favor cooling foods: cucumber, mung bean, watermelon, leafy greens.
Favor cooked, warm meals over raw/cold food for easier digestion, especially in the morning.
Eat with the season: root vegetables in winter, light greens in spring/summer.

techniques.title: Morning Qi Circulation Set
techniques.description: A short sequence of self-massage and gentle stretching done immediately upon waking to 'wake up' the body's energy.
steps: Rub palms together until warm, then cup over closed eyes.
Gently tap down the arms, torso, and legs with loose fists.
Rotate the neck and shoulders slowly in both directions.
Finish with 10 slow, deep breaths, hands resting on the lower belly.
benefits: Sets a calm tone for the day

techniques.title: Temazcal-Inspired Heat & Breath Ritual
techniques.description: The temazcal is a ceremonial sweat lodge for physical and spiritual cleansing. A home-adapted version uses heat, breath, and intention (not a substitute for an authentic ceremony with a guide).
steps: Take a hot shower or bath, setting an intention for what you want to release.
While in the heat, breathe slowly and deeply, visualizing tension leaving the body with each exhale.
Optional: burn copal or a similar resin nearby (in a ventilated space) as is traditional in ceremony.
After, drink water and sit quietly for a few minutes before returning to activity.
Note: for the full ceremonial experience, seek an authentic temazcal led by a trained practitioner.

techniques.title: Simplified Limpia (Energetic Cleansing)
techniques.description: A limpia is traditionally performed by a curandero/a using herbs, eggs, or smoke to clear negative energy. This is a simplified self-practice version for daily use, not a replacement for a full ceremony.
steps: Stand or sit quietly and name what you want to release (a worry, a bad interaction, tension).
Use a bundle of rosemary or other aromatic herb; pass it around your body from head to feet (or use smoke from copal/palo santo in a ventilated space).
Speak an intention aloud, e.g. 'I release what does not serve me.'
Finish by washing your hands and face with cool water.

techniques.title: Tila & Manzanilla (Calming Herbal Teas)
techniques.description: Tila (linden flower) and manzanilla (chamomile) are traditional Mexican remedies for anxiety, poor sleep, and stomach upset.
steps: Steep 1-2 tsp dried tila or manzanilla flowers in hot water for 5-10 minutes.
Drink in the evening to support calm and sleep, or after meals for digestion.
Can be combined with a drop of honey.
Note: consult a doctor if pregnant, nursing, or on medication, as herbal remedies can interact with treatments.

techniques.title: Traditional Mexican Whole-Food Principle (Maíz, Frijol, Chile)
techniques.description: The traditional Mesoamerican diet centers on nixtamalized corn, beans, and chile — a nutritionally complete, whole-food combination refined over centuries.
steps: Favor nixtamalized corn products (traditional tortillas, tamales) over refined flour where possible.
Pair corn with beans regularly — together they form a complete protein.
Include fresh chile, tomato, and herbs like epazote for flavor and micronutrients rather than heavy processed sauces.
Cook meals from whole ingredients rather than pre-packaged versions when practical.

techniques.title: Anapanasati (Breath Awareness Meditation)
techniques.description: One of the foundational Buddhist meditations: simply observing the natural breath without controlling it, to train sustained attention.
steps: Sit comfortably with a straight but relaxed spine.
Close your eyes and bring attention to the sensation of breath at the nostrils or belly.
Don't control the breath — just notice it as it naturally happens.
When the mind wanders, gently return attention to the breath, without judgment.
Start with 5-10 minutes and build up over time.

techniques.title: Metta (Loving-Kindness Meditation)
techniques.description: A structured meditation for cultivating goodwill toward yourself and others, used to soften self-criticism and reduce interpersonal resentment.
steps: Sit quietly and silently repeat: 'May I be happy. May I be healthy. May I be at ease.'
After a few minutes, bring to mind someone you love and repeat the same phrases for them.
Extend to a neutral person, then (optionally) someone you have difficulty with.
Finish by extending the phrases to 'all beings.'

techniques.title: Walking Meditation (Kinhin)
techniques.description: A slow, deliberate walking practice used between sitting meditations to maintain mindfulness while in motion.
steps: Choose a quiet path, 10-20 steps long.
Walk slowly, feeling the sensation of each foot lifting, moving, and placing down.
Keep hands clasped or relaxed at your sides; eyes softly lowered.
At the end of the path, pause, turn, and continue.
Practice for 5-15 minutes, especially useful when sitting still feels hard.

techniques.title: Dinacharya (Ayurvedic Daily Routine)
techniques.description: A structured daily routine believed to align the body with natural rhythms, reducing stress and improving energy and digestion.
steps: Wake before sunrise (or consistently early) rather than sleeping in.
Scrape the tongue and drink a glass of warm water upon waking.
Practice a few minutes of stretching or gentle movement before eating.
Eat the largest meal at midday when digestion is considered strongest.
Wind down with no screens for 30-60 minutes before a consistent bedtime.

techniques.title: Abhyanga (Self Warm-Oil Massage)
techniques.description: A daily self-massage with warm oil, traditionally used to calm the nervous system and improve circulation.
steps: Warm a neutral oil (sesame is traditional) slightly.
Massage into scalp, then work down the body toward the heart in long strokes on limbs, circular on joints.
Let the oil sit for 5-10 minutes if possible.
Shower with warm water, using minimal soap to leave a light residue.

techniques.title: Shinrin-Yoku (Forest Bathing)
techniques.origin: Japan (developed 1980s, rooted in Shinto/Zen nature reverence)
techniques.description: A practice of unhurried, sensory immersion in nature, distinct from exercise or hiking — the goal is presence, not distance covered.
steps: Go to a natural area (a park is fine) with no destination or pace goal.
Walk slowly, deliberately noticing sounds, smells, textures, and light.
Pause and sit for several minutes, simply observing surroundings.
Leave phone notifications off; the point is unstructured sensory attention.
Aim for at least 20-40 minutes.

techniques.title: Zazen (Seated Zen Meditation)
techniques.description: The core sitting meditation of Zen practice, emphasizing upright posture and open awareness rather than a specific focus object.
steps: Sit on a cushion or chair with an upright, dignified posture.
Rest hands in your lap, one on top of the other, thumbs lightly touching.
Keep eyes slightly open, gaze low, unfocused.
Breathe naturally; let thoughts arise and pass without engaging them.
Practice for a set period (start with 10 minutes), often marked with a bell.

techniques.title: Monastic Simplicity Eating Principle
techniques.description: Shaolin monks traditionally eat a simple, plant-based diet, viewed as supporting both physical training and mental clarity.
steps: Build meals around vegetables, grains (rice, noodles), and tofu/legumes rather than heavy meat.
Eat until about 80% full, stopping before feeling stuffed.
Eat at consistent times, avoiding late heavy meals before training or sleep.
Minimize processed/fried food in favor of simply prepared whole ingredients.

techniques.title: Inner Smile Meditation
techniques.description: A visualization practice where you direct a feeling of warmth/smiling attention to each internal organ, traditionally believed to relax the body and settle emotion.
steps: Sit comfortably and bring a slight smile to your face, even if it feels artificial at first.
Direct that 'smiling' warm attention to your eyes, then down to the heart, lungs, liver, and stomach in turn.
Pause a few breaths at each area, noticing any tension and letting it soften.
Finish by resting attention on the lower belly (dantian) for a minute.

techniques.title: Sahumerio Breath & Smoke Ritual
techniques.description: A grounding ritual pairing slow breath with copal or herb smoke, traditionally used to mark a transition (start of day, entering a space, after conflict).
steps: Light copal resin or a dried herb bundle in a heatproof dish (ventilated space or outdoors).
Stand a comfortable distance away and take slow breaths, allowing the scent to arrive naturally (don't force smoke inhalation).
With each exhale, mentally release one specific tension or worry.
Close with three slow breaths of gratitude before returning to activity.

techniques.title: Mindful Eating Practice
techniques.description: Eating slowly and with full attention, traditionally used to build present-moment awareness and a healthier relationship with food.
steps: Before eating, pause for one breath and silently acknowledge the food in front of you.
Eat without screens or reading; place utensils down between bites.
Notice texture, flavor, and temperature fully for the first few bites.
Check in partway through the meal on actual hunger/fullness rather than eating on autopilot.

techniques.title: Nadi Shodhana (Alternate Nostril Breathing)
techniques.description: A balancing breath technique traditionally used to calm the nervous system and clear the mind before focused work or sleep.
steps: Sit comfortably, spine tall.
Close the right nostril with the right thumb, inhale slowly through the left nostril.
Close the left nostril with the ring finger, release the thumb, exhale through the right nostril.
Inhale through the right, then switch and exhale through the left. This completes one round.
Repeat for 5-10 rounds.

techniques.title: Eating for Your Dosha (Constitution)
techniques.description: Ayurveda suggests adjusting diet based on constitution type (Vata, Pitta, Kapha) rather than a single universal diet.
steps: If prone to anxiety, dry skin, or feeling 'scattered' (Vata-type), favor warm, moist, grounding foods like soups and cooked grains.
If prone to irritability or heartburn (Pitta-type), favor cooling foods and avoid excess spice/fried food.
If prone to sluggishness or weight gain (Kapha-type), favor lighter, warming, spiced foods and reduce heavy dairy/sugar.
Eat the main meal at midday and keep dinner lighter, regardless of type.

techniques.title: Ikigai Reflection
techniques.description: A reflective practice for identifying your 'reason for being' at the intersection of what you love, what you're good at, what the world needs, and what sustains you.
steps: Take a quiet 15 minutes with paper (not a screen).
Write short answers to: What do I love? What am I good at? What does the world need from me? What sustains me practically?
Look for overlaps between the answers rather than forcing one perfect answer.
Revisit and revise this every few months rather than treating it as fixed.

techniques.title: Seasonal, Small-Plate Eating (Shun)
techniques.description: Traditional Japanese eating emphasizes seasonal ingredients at their peak, served in smaller varied portions rather than one large dish.
steps: Favor whatever produce/fish is currently in season locally over out-of-season imports.
Serve meals as several small varied dishes rather than one large plate — encourages natural portion control.
Follow 'hara hachi bu' — eat until about 80% full.
Include fermented foods (miso, pickles) regularly for digestion.

techniques.title: Dichotomy of Control Reflection
techniques.description: A core Stoic exercise: explicitly sorting a worry into 'within my control' vs. 'not within my control' to reduce anxious rumination.
steps: When a worry arises, write it down plainly.
List what parts of it are within your control (your actions, effort, responses).
List what parts are not (others' opinions, outcomes, the past).
Redirect energy only toward the controllable list; consciously let go of effort on the rest.

techniques.title: Evening Review
techniques.description: A nightly reflection practice reviewing the day's actions honestly, without harsh self-judgment, to build self-awareness over time.
steps: At the end of the day, ask: What did I do well today? Where did I fall short? What will I do differently tomorrow?
Write brief honest answers (a few sentences each is enough).
Avoid self-punishment — the goal is clear-eyed observation, not guilt.
Keep entries in one place to notice patterns over weeks.

techniques.title: Negative Visualization (Premeditatio Malorum)
techniques.description: Briefly imagining the loss of something you value, not to induce fear, but to build genuine gratitude and reduce complacency.
steps: Choose something you have that you often take for granted (health, a relationship, your routine).
Spend 2-3 minutes imagining life without it, briefly and without dwelling in distress.
Return attention to the present, noticing gratitude for what is actually here now.
Use sparingly (a few times a week), not as constant anxious rehearsal.

techniques.title: Cold Water Immersion
techniques.description: Brief immersion in cold water, traditionally paired with sauna heat, used for circulation, mood, and resilience-building.
steps: If new to this, start with cold showers (30-60 seconds) rather than full immersion.
If doing sauna-to-cold contrast, warm thoroughly first, then immerse briefly (start with seconds, not minutes).
Breathe slowly and steadily through the initial shock rather than gasping.
Warm up gradually afterward with movement or dry layers rather than immediately re-heating artificially.
Note: consult a doctor first if you have cardiovascular conditions.

techniques.title: Sauna as Communal Reset
techniques.description: Regular sauna use, traditionally a communal and unhurried ritual, used for both physical recovery and social/mental decompression.
steps: Set aside unhurried time (20-30 min minimum) rather than treating it as a quick errand.
Sit in the heat in a few rounds (e.g. 10-15 min), cooling down between rounds with fresh air or a cool shower.
If possible, share the space with others without phones — this is traditionally a social, conversational ritual, not a solitary one.
Hydrate well before and after.

techniques.title: Seasonal Light Rhythm Adjustment
techniques.description: A practice of consciously adjusting activity and rest to extreme seasonal light/dark cycles rather than fighting them, traditional to Arctic Indigenous life.
steps: In dark winter months, prioritize getting bright light (outdoor or a light lamp) in the first hour of waking.
Accept a naturally slower, more restful pace in deep winter rather than forcing summer-level output.
In bright summer months, use blackout coverings to protect sleep despite long daylight.
Build in deliberate rest/reflection blocks during low-light seasons rather than treating them as 'lost' time.

techniques.title: Rhythmic Movement / Drum Release
techniques.origin: Yoruba and broader West African communal ritual tradition
techniques.description: Using rhythm (drumming, clapping, or dancing to rhythmic music) as a traditional means of emotional release and communal bonding.
steps: Play rhythmic music (drum-based if possible) and allow the body to move freely without choreography.
Focus on releasing a specific stored emotion (grief, frustration) through movement rather than performing for appearance.
If in a group setting, let the rhythm synchronize the group rather than each person moving in isolation.
Close with a few still, quiet breaths to transition back to calm.

techniques.title: Ancestral Gratitude Reflection
techniques.origin: Yoruba and broader West African ancestral-honoring traditions
techniques.description: A reflective practice of acknowledging those who came before you, traditionally used to build a sense of continuity, resilience, and belonging.
steps: Sit quietly and bring to mind a family member or ancestor (known or unknown by name) whose effort contributed to your life.
Silently or aloud, acknowledge specifically what you believe they endured or gave.
Consider one value or strength you carry that may trace back to them.
Close by stating an intention to carry that forward.

techniques.title: Communal Meal Practice
techniques.description: Eating from a shared dish/table as a deliberate communal act, traditionally reinforcing social bonds alongside nourishment.
steps: Where possible, eat at least one meal a day with others rather than alone or on a screen.
Use the meal as a time for conversation and presence, not multitasking.
If eating from shared dishes, let this reinforce a sense of trust and connection rather than rushing.
Express thanks aloud to whoever prepared the food.
